speaker: Jigar Shah
title: Jigar Shah on the DOE's Role In Accelerating The Energy Transition
question: In energy project finance, why do commercial banks still refuse to lend to a proven new asset class even after it builds a massive deal pipeline?
guest: When you think about where I was at in 2003, after we did the Goldman fund and we had a $500 million pipeline, you still had a hard time breaking through with banks. A lot of banks would say, 'Look, I don't get paid that much, and you're basically asking me to do something weird. I have to write 12 white papers to educate my investment committee on this new asset class, and it's so much easier for me just to do a really weird real estate deal. So why am I spending all this time on it?' Largely there isn't real technology risk—sometimes there's perceived technology risk—but most of the time it's just getting their attention. They really need someone to be first. So they come into the Loan Programs Office, we give them money first and do proper underwriting due diligence. After we do the first deal, a whole bunch of banks say, 'All right, we're happy to be the second money in because we can read the Department of Energy's white papers and we don't have to do that work.'

points.core: Bank resistance usually stems from internal organizational friction rather than real technology risk.
points.note: Accept: inertia, attention bottlenecks, or merely perceived rather than actual technical risk blocking bank loans. Do not credit: claims that banks reject deals solely because the technology is unproven or unprofitable.

points.core: Loan officers avoid unfamiliar asset classes because educating investment committees pays poorly.
points.note: Accept: asymmetric effort-to-compensation incentives where bankers prefer closing familiar deals (like real estate) over writing extensive diligence memos for a novel asset class. Do not credit: generic claims that banks are conservative or heavily regulated.

points.core: Commercial banks wait for a first-mover lender to establish the underwriting playbook.
points.note: Accept: banks preferring to be 'second money in' after a public lender or anchor underwriter absorbs the initial technical due diligence and documentation. Do not credit: generic calls for government subsidies or loan guarantees without the diligence-precedent mechanism.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Because a pipeline shows demand for capital, not evidence of repayment. Project finance lenders are non-recourse, thinly compensated senior creditors with no upside, so they underwrite the downside, and that requires things a pipeline cannot supply.

The first is operating history: years of performance data across many projects, through stress conditions, showing how the technology degrades, what it costs to maintain, and how often it fails. "Proven" technically is not the same as proven statistically over a 15–20 year loan tenor.

The second is contracted, predictable cash flow. New asset classes often rely on merchant revenues, novel offtake structures, or policy-dependent incomes (battery storage and hydrogen are typical examples), which banks cannot size debt against with confidence.

The third is a standardised risk allocation: creditworthy EPC wraps, warranties, insurance products, independent engineers with benchmarks, rating-agency methodologies, and precedent documentation that credit committees recognise.

Finally, there is little default and recovery data, which regulatory capital models and credit committees need.

So the gap is typically bridged first by sponsors' equity, development banks, export credit agencies, and government guarantees, until a track record of closed and performing deals accumulates.

points.why: The response attributes bank resistance to gaps in evidence about performance, repayment, and recovery without identifying internal organizational friction as the usual cause.
The response ties thin compensation to lenders’ focus on downside risk and gives no causal role to loan officers’ incentives to avoid educating credit committees.

The response describes early financing as a bridge to a track record of performing deals without explaining how a first lender’s due diligence and documentation give commercial banks an underwriting playbook.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Commercial banks provide low-margin, non-recourse debt repaid solely from project cash flows, exposing them to full downside risk with no equity upside. Consequently, proven technology and market demand do not equal bankability. Even with a massive deal pipeline, credit committees and banking regulations require years of real-world operating, degradation, and default data across economic cycles to underwrite long-term cash flows. New asset classes lack this actuarial history and the risk-transfer ecosystem banks demand: standardized, investment-grade offtake contracts, predictable collateral values, and creditworthy construction and performance guarantees from major counterparties.

Moreover, early pipelines are often fragmented and bespoke. Until contracts and technical standards converge, steep legal and engineering due-diligence costs make underwriting uneconomical against thin lending spreads, especially on smaller deals. Finally, commercial banks rely on recycling capital; without established credit-rating methodologies and institutional takeout buyers, they cannot easily syndicate or securitize these loans, trapping illiquid, capital-intensive assets on their balance sheets.

points.why: The response attributes bank resistance to gaps in operating data, contracts, and risk transfer, leaving internal inertia and attention bottlenecks unaddressed.
The response links thin lending spreads to legal and engineering costs without explaining why loan officers favor familiar deals over the poorly rewarded work of educating credit committees.
The response identifies missing standards and takeout buyers without explaining how a first lender’s documented underwriting would make later banks willing to lend.

noweb.answer: Commercial banks provide low-margin, non-recourse debt with no equity upside, meaning a massive deal pipeline cannot compensate for unquantifiable downside risk. Even when a technology works physically, "proven" is not the same as "bankable." Project finance lenders require multi-year, commercial-scale operating data so independent engineers can validate degradation, availability, and worst-case cash flows to size debt service coverage ratios. New asset classes lack this actuarial history as well as creditworthy risk allocation. Early manufacturers and contractors rarely have the balance sheets to backstop fixed-price construction wraps or long-term performance warranties, while revenues often rely on merchant exposure, short tenors, or unrated buyers rather than twenty-year, investment-grade offtake agreements. Meanwhile, institutional and regulatory rules penalize novelty: Basel capital charges, rigid credit committees, unstandardized contracts, and illiquid syndication markets make bespoke underwriting uneconomic for thin lending spreads. Until public green banks, insurers, and higher-yield infrastructure funds standardize documentation and establish multi-year performance records, commercial banks remain on the sidelines regardless of pipeline volume.

points.why: The response centers on unquantified downside and missing performance data, with internal friction presented as an additional barrier.
The response discusses thin lending spreads but does not explain why loan officers prefer familiar deals over the poorly rewarded work of educating credit committees.
The response calls for standardized documents and longer performance records but does not explain how banks rely on a first lender’s underwriting and diligence.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
A pipeline shows that people want to build the projects. It doesn't show that the projects can repay a loan, and repayment is the only thing a commercial bank's credit committee is judging. Project finance lenders size debt against the asset's future cash flows, so they want years of operating data showing how the asset actually performs: degradation, availability, O&M costs, and how revenue holds up through market cycles. A new asset class, such as early offshore wind, merchant battery storage, or green hydrogen, has announced deals but few operating years, so there is no default or recovery history to price against.

Banks also look for bankable revenue, meaning long-term offtake contracts with creditworthy buyers. New sectors often depend on merchant or policy-driven revenue instead. Equipment warranties, insurance and contract templates aren't standardized yet, and suppliers may be thinly capitalized. Regulatory capital rules make unrated, unfamiliar exposures expensive to hold, and no credit officer wants to approve the first loss in an untested category. Banks don't want to be first, so the usual path is public lenders, export credit agencies, guarantees or patient equity funding the early projects. Commercial debt follows once a performance record exists.

points.why: The response attributes bank resistance to repayment uncertainty and limited operating history without identifying internal organizational friction as the usual barrier.
The response never connects the effort of educating credit committees to loan officers’ compensation or their incentive to pursue familiar deals.
The response says banks wait for a performance record and omits how a first lender’s diligence and documentation give later lenders a reusable underwriting precedent.

models.answer: In energy project finance, commercial banks lend on a non-recourse basis for thin, fixed margins, meaning they capture no equity upside while bearing full downside risk if a project fails. Because of this asymmetric payoff, technical viability and a large pipeline are not enough to satisfy credit committees. A pipeline reflects developer ambition, not bankable cash flows. Banks require multi-year, commercial-scale operating data to model degradation, availability, and default rates, which new asset classes lack even after early deployments succeed. They also insist on standardized risk allocation: fixed-price, date-certain construction wraps from creditworthy contractors, proven insurance coverage, and long-term offtake contracts with investment-grade buyers rather than merchant revenue exposure. Without deep historical loss data and established secondary markets for syndication or refinancing, regulatory capital rules force banks to hold more capital against the loans, eroding returns. Until revenue certainty, contractual risk transfer, and actuarial track records mature, commercial banks leave the asset class to equity investors, development banks, and private credit.
